claim: Cognitive control proactively configures information processing to suit expected task demands.
source: Cognitive control proactively configures information processing to suit expected task demands.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract that is supported by the entire study design and results.

claim: Predictions of forthcoming demand can be driven by explicit external cues.
source: Predictions of forthcoming demand can be driven by explicit external cues or be generated internally, based on past experience (cognitive history).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental design using pre-cues and by behavioral data showing cue effects.

claim: Predictions of forthcoming demand can be generated internally, based on past experience (cognitive history).
source: Predictions of forthcoming demand can be driven by explicit external cues or be generated internally, based on past experience (cognitive history).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental findings showing trial history effects on behavior.

claim: External and internally generated predictions jointly guide task preparation.
source: Pairing a probabilistic task-switching paradigm with computational modeling, we found that external and internally generated predictions jointly guide task preparation, with a bias for internal predictions.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by computational modeling and behavioral data.

claim: There is a bias for internal predictions over external predictions in guiding task preparation.
source: Pairing a probabilistic task-switching paradigm with computational modeling, we found that external and internally generated predictions jointly guide task preparation, with a bias for internal predictions.
evidence: This is supported by the finding that β was significantly lower than 0.5, indicating stronger reliance on internal predictions.

claim: The two sources of task prediction are integrated in dorsolateral prefrontal cortex.
source: Using model-based neuroimaging, we then show that the two sources of task prediction are integrated in dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, and jointly inform a representation of the likelihood of a change in task demand, encoded in frontoparietal cortex.
evidence: This is supported by fMRI MVPA results showing encoding of Pjoint in dlPFC.

claim: Integrated task predictions jointly inform a representation of the likelihood of a change in task demand, encoded in frontoparietal cortex.
source: Using model-based neuroimaging, we then show that the two sources of task prediction are integrated in dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, and jointly inform a representation of the likelihood of a change in task demand, encoded in frontoparietal cortex.
evidence: This is supported by fMRI findings showing encoding of proactive switch demand in frontoparietal regions.

claim: Dorsomedial prefrontal cortex encodes the need for reactive task-set adjustment upon task-stimulus onset.
source: Upon task-stimulus onset, dorsomedial prefrontal cortex encoded the need for reactive task-set adjustment.
evidence: This is supported by fMRI findings showing encoding of PEjoint in dmPFC/ACC.

claim: Cognitive control allows humans to flexibly switch or update task-sets.
source: For instance, depending on current goals, humans can flexibly switch or update 'task-sets' that allow them to shift between different aspects of a stimulus to which they attend and respond (Monsell, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: A task-set involves the mental representation of task-relevant stimuli, responses, and their corresponding stimulus-response mappings.
source: Here, a task-set involves the mental representation of task-relevant stimuli, responses, and their corresponding stimulus-response mappings, allowing for an appropriate action to be executed in response to a stimulus (cf. Monsell, 2003; Kiesel et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Controlled processing is slow and effortful.
source: Cognitive control thus grants the organism considerable behavioral flexibility, but it also incurs costs, in that controlled processing is slow and effortful (Norman and Shallice, 1986)
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: It takes longer to perform a trial when a shift in the task-set is required than when staying with the same set.
source: to wit, it takes longer to perform a trial when a shift in the task-set is required than when staying with the same set –– known as 'switch costs' –– which is thought to reflect additional cognitive processing, including the updating of the task-set and the resolution of proactive interference (i.e., the previously activated task-set's interference with the retrieval of the currently required task-set) (Rogers and Monsell, 1995; Badre and Wagner, 2006).
evidence: This is the classic switch cost effect, supported by citations and replicated in the current study.

claim: Switch costs reflect additional cognitive processing, including the updating of the task-set and the resolution of proactive interference.
source: to wit, it takes longer to perform a trial when a shift in the task-set is required than when staying with the same set –– known as 'switch costs' –– which is thought to reflect additional cognitive processing, including the updating of the task-set and the resolution of proactive interference (i.e., the previously activated task-set's interference with the retrieval of the currently required task-set) (Rogers and Monsell, 1995; Badre and Wagner, 2006).
evidence: This is an interpretation of switch costs supported by citations.

claim: People predict forthcoming task demands and adjust processing accordingly.
source: The broad suggestion is that people predict forthcoming task demands and adjust processing accordingly (e.g., Shenhav et al., 2013; Egner, 2014; Jiang et al., 2014; Abrahamse et al., 2016; Waskom et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Expectations about task demands can be driven by explicit predictions provided by external cues.
source: Importantly, such expectations about task demands can be driven by two sources: explicit predictions provided by external cues (Rogers and Monsell, 1995; Dreisbach et al., 2002; Badre and Wagner, 2006) and internally generated, trial history-based predictions, which are typically implicit (Dreisbach and Haider, 2006; Mayr, 2006; Bugg and Crump, 2012; Egner, 2014; Chiu and Egner, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Expectations about task demands can be driven by internally generated, trial history-based predictions, which are typically implicit.
source: Importantly, such expectations about task demands can be driven by two sources: explicit predictions provided by external cues (Rogers and Monsell, 1995; Dreisbach et al., 2002; Badre and Wagner, 2006) and internally generated, trial history-based predictions, which are typically implicit (Dreisbach and Haider, 2006; Mayr, 2006; Bugg and Crump, 2012; Egner, 2014; Chiu and Egner, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Trial history based predictions impact cognitive control even in cases where these predictions are redundant, as in the presence of 100% valid external cues.
source: In particular, trial history based predictions impact cognitive control even in cases where these predictions are redundant, as in the presence of 100% valid external cues for selecting the correct control strategy (e.g., Alpay et al., 2009; Correa et al., 2009; Kemper et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior behavioral studies.

claim: Participants performed with high accuracy in the color task (0.87 ± 0.02).
source: Participants performed with high accuracy (color task: 0.87 ± 0.02 [mean ±SEM]; motion task: 0.88 ± 0.02), which did not differ between tasks (t21 = 0.30, p=0.75).
evidence: This is a direct report of behavioral data.

claim: Participants performed with high accuracy in the motion task (0.88 ± 0.02).
source: Participants performed with high accuracy (color task: 0.87 ± 0.02 [mean ±SEM]; motion task: 0.88 ± 0.02), which did not differ between tasks (t21 = 0.30, p=0.75).
evidence: This is a direct report of behavioral data.

claim: Accuracy did not differ between color and motion tasks.
source: Participants performed with high accuracy (color task: 0.87 ± 0.02 [mean ±SEM]; motion task: 0.88 ± 0.02), which did not differ between tasks (t21 = 0.30, p=0.75).
evidence: This is supported by statistical test results.

claim: There was a significant interaction between previous- and current-trial tasks in accuracy.
source: Replicating the classic task switch cost, there was a significant interaction between previous- and current-trial tasks in both accuracy (F1,21=47.0, p<0.001; Figure 2A) and RT (F1,21=95.5, p<0.001; Figure 2B)
evidence: This is supported by statistical test results and Figure 2A.

claim: There was a significant interaction between previous- and current-trial tasks in RT.
source: Replicating the classic task switch cost, there was a significant interaction between previous- and current-trial tasks in both accuracy (F1,21=47.0, p<0.001; Figure 2A) and RT (F1,21=95.5, p<0.001; Figure 2B)
evidence: This is supported by statistical test results and Figure 2B.

claim: Task-repeat trials had higher accuracy (0.90 ± 0.01) than task-switch trials (0.85 ± 0.02).
source: driven by more accurate (task-repeat accuracy: 0.90 ± 0.01; task-switch accuracy: 0.85 ± 0.02) and faster responses (task-repeat RT: 0.87 ± 0.01 s; task-switch RT: 0.94 ± 0.02 s) when the task repeated than when it switched.
evidence: This is a direct report of behavioral data.

claim: Task-repeat trials had faster responses (0.87 ± 0.01 s) than task-switch trials (0.94 ± 0.02 s).
source: driven by more accurate (task-repeat accuracy: 0.90 ± 0.01; task-switch accuracy: 0.85 ± 0.02) and faster responses (task-repeat RT: 0.87 ± 0.01 s; task-switch RT: 0.94 ± 0.02 s) when the task repeated than when it switched.
evidence: This is a direct report of behavioral data.

claim: Motion trials were faster than color trials.
source: Additionally, motion trials were faster than color trials (F1,21=21.3, p<0.001; Figure 2B; motion RT: 0.84 ± 0.02 s; color RT: 0.97 ± 0.02 s), which is consistent with previous studies using similar color/motion discrimination tasks and dot cloud stimuli (Jiang et al., 2016; Waskom et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by statistical test results and is consistent with prior literature.

claim: There was a significant effect of the explicit pre-cue on RT.
source: Most importantly, there was a significant effect of the explicit pre-cue, as reflected by a main effect of task prediction on RT (F4,84=4.3, p<0.005; Figure 2D), with response speed scaling with predictive pre-cue information.
evidence: This is supported by statistical test results and Figure 2D.

claim: Response speed scaled with predictive pre-cue information.
source: Most importantly, there was a significant effect of the explicit pre-cue, as reflected by a main effect of task prediction on RT (F4,84=4.3, p<0.005; Figure 2D), with response speed scaling with predictive pre-cue information.
evidence: This is supported by the main effect of task prediction on RT.

claim: The interaction between the prior trial task-sets (trial i-2) and the current task was significant in both accuracy and RT.
source: The interaction between the prior trial task-sets and the current task was significant in both accuracy (F1,21=6.2, p=0.02; Figure 2E) and RT (F1,21=73.2, p<0.001; Figure 2F) for trial i-2.
evidence: This is supported by statistical test results and Figures 2E and 2F.

claim: For trial i-3, the interaction between prior trial task-set and current task was significant in RT but not in accuracy.
source: For trial i-3, the interaction was not significant in accuracy (F1,21<1, n.s.; Figure 2G), but was significant in RT (F1,21=8.4, p=0.008; Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by statistical test results and Figures 2G and 2H.

claim: Trial i-4 did not show a modulation effect in either accuracy or RT.
source: Trial i-4 did not show a modulation effect in either accuracy or RT (both F1,21<1, n.s).
evidence: This is supported by statistical test results.

claim: The modulation effect decayed as the distance from previous trial to current trial increased.
source: Since the modulation effect decayed as the distance from previous trial to current trial increased (Figure 2A–B and E–H), trials beyond i-4 were not tested.
evidence: This is supported by the pattern of results shown in Figures 2A-B and E-H.

claim: Trial-history based task predictions stemming from learning over the last three trials impact behavior.
source: These results provide strong evidence that trial-history based task predictions –– stemming from learning over the last three trials –– impact behavior, biasing participants towards expecting task repetitions.
evidence: This is an inference from the behavioral data showing effects up to trial i-3.

claim: Trial-history based task predictions bias participants towards expecting task repetitions.
source: These results provide strong evidence that trial-history based task predictions –– stemming from learning over the last three trials –– impact behavior, biasing participants towards expecting task repetitions.
evidence: This is an inference from the behavioral pattern showing hot-hand fallacy effects.

claim: The joint-guidance model outperformed all other models with a protected exceedance probability of 0.997.
source: The joint-guidance model clearly outperformed all other models, with a protected exceedance probability of 0.997, indicating that behavior was best explained by a collective contribution to proactive task-set updating from cue-induced and internally generated task predictions.
evidence: This is supported by Bayesian model comparison results.

claim: Behavior was best explained by a collective contribution to proactive task-set updating from cue-induced and internally generated task predictions.
source: The joint-guidance model clearly outperformed all other models, with a protected exceedance probability of 0.997, indicating that behavior was best explained by a collective contribution to proactive task-set updating from cue-induced and internally generated task predictions.
evidence: This is an inference from the model comparison results.

claim: The mean learning rate was 0.52.
source: The mean learning rate was 0.52, indicating that, on average, participants weighted the i-1 trial about as much as the prior trial history in determining the internally generated task prediction.
evidence: This is a direct report of modeling results.

claim: On average, participants weighted the i-1 trial about as much as the prior trial history in determining the internally generated task prediction.
source: The mean learning rate was 0.52, indicating that, on average, participants weighted the i-1 trial about as much as the prior trial history in determining the internally generated task prediction.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the learning rate value.

claim: The effect of trial history on behavior was on average 3 times as strong as that of the cue-induced task prediction.
source: Strikingly, we found that even though trial history was not predictive of the forthcoming task, its effect on behavior was on average 3 times as strong as that of the cue-induced task prediction (group mean β: 0.26; range: 0-0.61; one sample t-test against 0.5: t21 = 5.42, P < 0.001; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the β parameter estimates and statistical tests.

claim: The group mean β was 0.26.
source: Strikingly, we found that even though trial history was not predictive of the forthcoming task, its effect on behavior was on average 3 times as strong as that of the cue-induced task prediction (group mean β: 0.26; range: 0-0.61; one sample t-test against 0.5: t21 = 5.42, P < 0.001; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a direct report of modeling results.

claim: Five participants showed either no or very little reliance on cue-induced task prediction.
source: Notably, five participants showed either no (β = 0, four subjects) or very little (β = 0.02, one subject) reliance on cue-induced task prediction.
evidence: This is a direct report of modeling results.

claim: After excluding participants with no or very little reliance on cue-induced prediction, the mean β of the remaining 17 participants remained significantly lower than 0.5.
source: Even after excluding these participants (to rule out the possibility that the differential reliance on trial history was due to a failure to understand the associations between the pictorial pre-cue and the task-set prediction), the mean β of the remaining 17 participants remained significantly lower than 0.5 (t16=3.96, P = 0.001), again indicating stronger reliance on the internally generated task prediction.
evidence: This is supported by statistical test results on a subset of participants.

claim: β estimates were significantly correlated between the first and last 3 runs.
source: To test the robustness of the β estimates, we computed β separately using the first and last 3 runs. Across subjects, β estimates were significantly correlated between these two task phases (r = 0.63, p = 0.002), suggesting reliable β estimation within participants.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis.

claim: There was no significant difference in β estimates between the first and last 3 runs.
source: Also, there was no significant difference in β estimates between the first and last 3 runs (t21=1.32, p = 0.20), suggesting that the reliance on Pcue relative to Pint remained unchanged throughout the 9 runs in the fMRI session.
evidence: This is supported by statistical test results.

claim: The reliance on Pcue relative to Pint remained unchanged throughout the 9 runs in the fMRI session.
source: Also, there was no significant difference in β estimates between the first and last 3 runs (t21=1.32, p = 0.20), suggesting that the reliance on Pcue relative to Pint remained unchanged throughout the 9 runs in the fMRI session.
evidence: This is an inference from the lack of difference in β estimates over time.

claim: The mean estimated gain of RT was positively correlated with β estimates in the motion task.
source: Across participants, the mean estimated gain of RT was positively correlated with β estimates in both the motion (r = 0.74, p<0.001; Figure 3E) and color (r = 0.46, p=0.03; Figure 3F) tasks, indicating a clear behavioral benefit for relying on the external cue.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis and Figure 3E.

claim: The mean estimated gain of RT was positively correlated with β estimates in the color task.
source: Across participants, the mean estimated gain of RT was positively correlated with β estimates in both the motion (r = 0.74, p<0.001; Figure 3E) and color (r = 0.46, p=0.03; Figure 3F) tasks, indicating a clear behavioral benefit for relying on the external cue.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis and Figure 3F.

claim: There is a clear behavioral benefit for relying on the external cue.
source: Across participants, the mean estimated gain of RT was positively correlated with β estimates in both the motion (r = 0.74, p<0.001; Figure 3E) and color (r = 0.46, p=0.03; Figure 3F) tasks, indicating a clear behavioral benefit for relying on the external cue.
evidence: This is an inference from the positive correlation between β and RT gain.

claim: Relying on internally generated, trial history-based task prediction is sub-optimal in the present context.
source: This analysis underlines the sub-optimal nature of relying on internally generated, trial history-based task prediction in the present context.
evidence: This is an inference from the behavioral benefit analysis showing that higher reliance on external cues leads to better performance.

claim: The seemingly irrational reliance on internally generated task prediction may be attributable to a relatively lower cost of using internally generated control predictions compared to using cue-based predictions.
source: We speculate that this seemingly irrational reliance on internally generated task prediction may be attributable to a relatively lower cost (e.g., due to high automaticity) of using internally generated control predictions compared to using cue-based predictions (cf. Shenhav et al., 2013; Shenhav et al., 2017; see Discussion).
evidence: This is speculation based on the EVC model and the observed behavioral patterns.

claim: Left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) shows significantly above-chance encoding of the joint task prediction.
source: This analysis produced a map of the spatial distribution of the representation strength of Pjoint, exclusively revealing a left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) region centered on the middle frontal gyrus (MFG) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI MVPA results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The dlPFC results were not driven by univariate effects of task difficulty.
source: Thus, the dlPFC results were not driven by univariate effects of task difficulty.
evidence: This is supported by control analyses showing no significant univariate encoding of Pjoint in dlPFC.

claim: Pjoint better accounted for dlPFC fMRI activity patterns than other mixtures of Pint and Pcue.
source: The mean of this null distribution was significantly smaller than the largest cluster size obtained using behaviorally derived βs (P = 0.02), suggesting that Pjoint better accounted for dlPFC fMRI activity patterns than other mixtures of Pint and Pcue.
evidence: This is supported by permutation testing comparing Pjoint to randomly sampled β parameters.

claim: The group mean encoding strength of Pjoint was significantly stronger than the chance level derived from random sampling procedure.
source: The group mean encoding strength (i.e., how well the fMRI data in the searchlights fit the model variable in a cross-validation procedure) of Pjoint was significantly stronger than the chance level derived from this random sampling procedure (P = 0.02, Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by permutation testing shown in Figure 4D.

claim: There is a significant negative correlation between β~s' distance from β and its encoding strength of how well the fMRI data fit the pseudo-Pjoint.
source: Supporting the idea of β representing a local maximum, we observed a significant negative correlation between β~s' distance from β and its encoding strength of how well the fMRI data fit the pseudo-Pjoint (r = -0.37, P < 0.001; Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: dlPFC plays a specific role in integrating joint predictions of forthcoming task demand.
source: Thus, these results offer strong evidence for a specific role of this dlPFC region in integrating joint predictions of forthcoming task demand, and against the alternative possibility that explicit externally and (likely implicit) internally generated predictions might drive task-set updating independently, without being integrated.
evidence: This is an inference from the selective encoding of Pjoint in dlPFC.

claim: Proactive switch demand is encoded in right frontopolar cortex (FPC), left inferior frontal gyrus (IFG), left precentral gyrus, bilateral supplementary motor area (SMA), left inferior parietal lobule/intraparietal sulcus (IPL/IPS), bilateral superior parietal lobule (SPL), precuneus, bilateral insula, bilateral putamen, bilateral lingual gyrus, and bilateral middle occipital gyrus.
source: Areas encoding switch demand included right frontopolar cortex (FPC, BA 10), left inferior frontal gyrus (IFG, pars opercularis), left precentral gyrus, bilateral supplementary motor area (SMA), left inferior parietal lobule/intraparietal sulcus (IPL/IPS), bilateral superior parietal lobule (SPL), precuneus, bilateral insula and the bilateral putamen of the dorsal striatum. This network extended well into visual cortex, including bilateral lingual gyrus and bilateral middle occipital gyrus, suggesting that participants also used task predictions to adjust visual processing of forthcoming information.
evidence: This is supported by fMRI MVPA results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Participants used task predictions to adjust visual processing of forthcoming information.
source: This network extended well into visual cortex, including bilateral lingual gyrus and bilateral middle occipital gyrus, suggesting that participants also used task predictions to adjust visual processing of forthcoming information.
evidence: This is an inference from the encoding of proactive switch demand in visual cortex.

claim: The frontoparietal control network is engaged in predicting control demands in the shape of representing the degree to which a current set has to be updated to suit the forthcoming task.
source: The present results move beyond these findings by showing that more than just encoding a currently active task rule, the frontoparietal control network is engaged in predicting control demands, in the shape of representing the degree to which a current set has to be updated to suit the forthcoming task (or switch likelihood).
evidence: This is an inference from the encoding of proactive switch demand in frontoparietal regions.

claim: Encoding of the prediction error associated with joint prediction was found in the dmPFC/ACC.
source: After the onset of the task cue and task stimulus, encoding of the prediction error associated with that joint prediction was found in the dmPFC/ACC, which is consistent with a large literature demonstrating ACC and dmPFC encoding of prediction error in a variety of different contexts (Holroyd and Coles, 2002; Ito et al., 2003; Matsumoto et al., 2007; Alexander and Brown, 2011; Ullsperger et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI results and is consistent with prior literature.

claim: Reactive switch demand is encoded in left dmPFC (including the ACC), bilateral precentral and postcentral gyrus, precuneus, right SPL, left inferior occipital gyrus, and IFG.
source: This analysis revealed encoding of PEjoint in a set of regions consisting of left dmPFC (including the ACC), bilateral precentral and postcentral gyrus, precuneus, right SPL, left inferior occipital gyrus, and IFG (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI MVPA results shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The dmPFC showed significantly above-chance encoding strength for PEjoint compared to randomly sampled βs.
source: Compared to randomly sampled βs, the dmPFC (Figure 6B), right precentral and postcentral gyrus, and precuneus showed significantly above-chance encoding strength for PEjoint, with the dmPFC exhibiting the strongest effect.
evidence: This is supported by permutation testing results.

claim: The dmPFC exhibited the strongest effect in encoding PEjoint among regions showing strong encoding.
source: Compared to randomly sampled βs, the dmPFC (Figure 6B), right precentral and postcentral gyrus, and precuneus showed significantly above-chance encoding strength for PEjoint, with the dmPFC exhibiting the strongest effect.
evidence: This is a direct comparison of effect sizes across regions.

claim: The effects of PEjoint encoding remained above chance in the dmPFC when tested separately using motion trials.
source: The effects remained above chance in the dmPFC when tested separately using motion (P < 0.001;Figure 6C) and color trials (P = 0.03; Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by permutation testing on motion trials shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The effects of PEjoint encoding remained above chance in the dmPFC when tested separately using color trials.
source: The effects remained above chance in the dmPFC when tested separately using motion (P < 0.001;Figure 6C) and color trials (P = 0.03; Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by permutation testing on color trials shown in Figure 6D.

claim: For motion trials, the encoding strength of pseudo-PEjoint decreased as a function of its Euclidean distance from βs.
source: Furthermore, for a given set of β~s, the encoding strength of its corresponding pseudo-PEjoint decreased as a function of its Euclidean distance from βs for both motion (r = -0.51, P < 0.001; Figure 6E) and color trials (r = -0.29, P < 0.001; Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: For color trials, the encoding strength of pseudo-PEjoint decreased as a function of its Euclidean distance from βs.
source: Furthermore, for a given set of β~s, the encoding strength of its corresponding pseudo-PEjoint decreased as a function of its Euclidean distance from βs for both motion (r = -0.51, P < 0.001; Figure 6E) and color trials (r = -0.29, P < 0.001; Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The dmPFC/ACC is involved in the reactive updating of task demand predictions based on the joint-guidance of internally generated and externally provided cue information.
source: Thus, we obtained strong evidence for an involvement of the dmPFC/ACC in the reactive updating of task demand predictions based on the joint-guidance of internally generated and externally provided cue information.
evidence: This is an inference from the selective encoding of PEjoint in dmPFC/ACC.

claim: Robust encoding of PEint was observed in the frontoparietal control network and the adjacent parietal portion of the dorsal attention network.
source: In close correspondence to the results of Waskom et al., 2017, we observed robust encoding of PEint in the frontoparietal control network and the adjacent parietal portion of the dorsal attention network (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) (Yeo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI results shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The updating of internally generated task predictions derived from a non-predictive trial sequence recruits the same neural substrates as updating of task predictions in response to predictive trial sequences.
source: These data show that the updating of internally generated task predictions derived from a non-predictive trial sequence (in the current study) recruits the same neural substrates as updating of task predictions in response to predictive trial sequences (Waskom et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference from the similarity of neural substrates encoding PEint in the current study and Waskom et al., 2017.

claim: There is a clear temporal segregation between the frontoparietal encoding of the proactive switch demand at the onset of pre-cue and the dmPFC/ACC encoding of reactive switch demand when the cue and task stimulus were presented.
source: Our findings also exhibit a clear temporal segregation between the frontoparietal encoding of the proactive switch demand at the onset of pre-cue (Figure 5A) and the dmPFC/ACC encoding of reactive switch demand when the cue and task stimulus were presented (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by the different timing of encoding shown in Figures 5A and 6A.

claim: The lateral frontoparietal control network guides proactive control implementation.
source: The present results strongly suggest that the lateral frontoparietal control network guides proactive control implementation, whereas the dmPFC/ACC detects the prediction error of control demand prediction, and signals the need of (or perhaps implements) reactive control to match the actual (rather than anticipated) cognitive control demand.
evidence: This is an inference from the encoding of proactive switch demand in frontoparietal regions.

claim: The dmPFC/ACC detects the prediction error of control demand prediction, and signals the need of (or perhaps implements) reactive control to match the actual cognitive control demand.
source: The present results strongly suggest that the lateral frontoparietal control network guides proactive control implementation, whereas the dmPFC/ACC detects the prediction error of control demand prediction, and signals the need of (or perhaps implements) reactive control to match the actual (rather than anticipated) cognitive control demand.
evidence: This is an inference from the encoding of reactive switch demand (PEjoint) in dmPFC/ACC.

claim: Experientially acquired and explicitly cued expectations of control demand are reconciled in dlPFC and dmPFC to jointly guide the implementation of cognitive control.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that experientially acquired and explicitly cued expectations of control demand are reconciled in dlPFC and dmPFC to jointly guide the implementation of cognitive control.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the combined fMRI findings.

claim: The cue-induced prediction requires learning and retrieving the associations between an external graphical pre-cue and its corresponding task-set prediction, which may incur a higher cost than internally generated prediction.
source: First, the cue-induced prediction requires learning and retrieving the associations between an external graphical pre-cue and its corresponding task-set prediction, which may incur a higher cost than internally generated prediction.
evidence: This is speculation about the source of differential costs.

claim: Internally generated predictions that anticipate the near future to resemble the recent past represent a default cognitive strategy grounded in evolutionary adaptation to an environment of high temporal auto-correlation of sensory inputs.
source: Second, it is reasonable to assume that internally generated predictions that anticipate the near future to resemble the recent past represent a default cognitive strategy grounded in evolutionary adaptation to an environment of high temporal auto-correlation of sensory inputs (Dong and Atick, 1995).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Ongoing perception is strongly reliant on recent experience.
source: Accordingly, it has been shown that ongoing perception (Fischer and Whitney, 2014) and decision-making (Cheadle et al., 2014) are strongly reliant on recent experience.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Decision-making is strongly reliant on recent experience.
source: Accordingly, it has been shown that ongoing perception (Fischer and Whitney, 2014) and decision-making (Cheadle et al., 2014) are strongly reliant on recent experience.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The recent past is (implicitly) employed as a powerful predictor of the immediate future for cognitive control processes.
source: The present results suggest that the same is true for cognitive control processes: the recent past is (implicitly) employed as a powerful predictor of the immediate future (see Egner, 2014; Jiang et al., 2015b; Waskom et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference from the current results and is consistent with prior literature.

claim: If self-generated predictions of task demand represent a default mode of control regulation, their generation is likely cheap.
source: If such self-generated predictions of task demand represent a default mode of control regulation, their generation is likely cheap and, importantly, it may require substantial cognitive effort to override such predictions, which would be another means of rendering the use of the explicit external cue more costly.
evidence: This is speculation about the cost structure of control predictions.

claim: It may require substantial cognitive effort to override self-generated predictions, which would be another means of rendering the use of the explicit external cue more costly.
source: If such self-generated predictions of task demand represent a default mode of control regulation, their generation is likely cheap and, importantly, it may require substantial cognitive effort to override such predictions, which would be another means of rendering the use of the explicit external cue more costly.
evidence: This is speculation about the cost of overriding default predictions.

claim: The internally generated predictions observed here took the form of increased expectations of task repetition with increasing run length of a given task (hot-hand fallacy).
source: The internally generated predictions we observed here took the form of increased expectations of task repetition with increasing run length of a given task (also known as the 'hot-hand fallacy'; Gilovich et al., 1985).
evidence: This is an inference from the behavioral pattern showing bias towards task repetition.

claim: Previous work has demonstrated a dissociation between explicit outcome predictions following the gambler's fallacy and implicit predictions, as expressed in behavior, following the hot-hand fallacy.
source: The fact that we observed the former rather than the latter is in line with our assumption that the internal predictions we measure here are likely implicit in nature, as previous work has demonstrated a dissociation between explicit outcome predictions following the gambler's fallacy and implicit predictions, as expressed in behavior, following the hot-hand fallacy (Perruchet, 1985; Jiménez and Méndez, 2013; Perruchet, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The fact that internally generated predictions followed the hot-hand pattern corroborates that participants (likely implicitly) assumed the trial history to be non-random.
source: Thus, the fact that internally generated predictions followed the hot-hand pattern further corroborates that participants (likely implicitly) assumed the trial history to be non-random.
evidence: This is an inference from the hot-hand pattern observed in the data.

claim: The EVC model predicts that the relative reliance on internally vs. externally generated predictions will change as a function of the cost and/or the benefit of engaging the more informative externally generated predictions.
source: The EVC model also predicts that the relative reliance on internally vs. externally generated predictions, which are the outcome of a cost-benefit analysis, will change as a function of the cost and/or the benefit of engaging the more informative externally generated predictions.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the EVC model framework.

claim: dlPFC has a well-established role in representing task rules and strategies.
source: This is in line with this region's well-established role in representing task rules and strategies (for review, see Sakai, 2008; cf. Waskom et al., 2014; Waskom et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The frontoparietal control network, insula, and dorsal striatum have long been implicated in task-set regulation.
source: Additionally, based on this joint prediction, the anticipated switch demand or amount of required task-set updating was represented in the frontoparietal control network, insula, and dorsal striatum. These regions have long been implicated in task-set regulation, as revealed initially by studies comparing neural activity on task-switch with task-repeat cues or trials (reviewed in Ruge et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Recent studies have used multivariate pattern analysis to decode the currently active task-set from frontoparietal cortex.
source: and more recently by studies using multivariate pattern analysis to decode the currently active task-set from frontoparietal cortex (Woolgar et al., 2011; Waskom et al., 2014; Loose et al., 2017; Qiao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: There is a large literature demonstrating ACC and dmPFC encoding of prediction error in a variety of different contexts.
source: After the onset of the task cue and task stimulus, encoding of the prediction error associated with that joint prediction was found in the dmPFC/ACC, which is consistent with a large literature demonstrating ACC and dmPFC encoding of prediction error in a variety of different contexts (Holroyd and Coles, 2002; Ito et al., 2003; Matsumoto et al., 2007; Alexander and Brown, 2011; Ullsperger et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The ACC monitors performance and signals the need for adjustments in cognitive control.
source: The representation of joint prediction error also reflects the degree to which the task-set has to be updated reactively; thus, this finding is also consistent with the theory that the ACC monitors performance and signals the need for adjustments in cognitive control (Botvinick et al., 2001; Ridderinkhof et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The dual mechanisms of cognitive control framework distinguishes between proactive, anticipatory, and reactive, compensatory application of control.
source: Our findings also exhibit a clear temporal segregation between the frontoparietal encoding of the proactive switch demand at the onset of pre-cue (Figure 5A) and the dmPFC/ACC encoding of reactive switch demand when the cue and task stimulus were presented (Figure 6A). This temporal and functional differentiation maps closely onto the 'dual mechanisms of cognitive control' framework (Braver, 2012), which distinguishes between proactive, anticipatory, and reactive, compensatory application of control.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the dual mechanisms framework.

claim: In a recent study that explicitly distinguished between proactive and reactive control in a conflict task, a left IFG area overlapping the IFG area in Figure 5 was implicated in using proactive control demand predictions.
source: In support of this contention, in a recent study that explicitly distinguished between proactive and reactive control in a conflict task, a left IFG area overlapping the IFG area in Figure 5 was also implicated in using proactive control demand predictions (Jiang et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Disrupting function in left IFG using transcranial magnetic stimulation selectively diminished the effects of learned control predictions on behavior.
source: Furthermore, disrupting function in this area using transcranial magnetic stimulation selectively diminished the effects of learned control predictions on behavior (Muhle-Karbe et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The current findings suggest a novel extension of the EVC theory, where a cost/benefit optimization process is applicable to the stage where different inputs to the control demand prediction process are reconciled.
source: Finally, the current findings suggest a novel extension of the EVC theory, which originally addressed a cost/benefit analysis of engaging control after prediction of control demands are formed (Shenhav et al., 2013). The present results suggest that a cost/benefit optimization process is also applicable to the preceding stage, where different inputs to the control demand prediction process are reconciled.
evidence: This is a theoretical inference from the current findings.

claim: The demand prediction reconciliation process would precede the putative EVC calculation and should directly influence it in a unidirectional, hierarchical fashion.
source: This demand prediction reconciliation process would not only precede the putative EVC calculation, but should also directly influence it, and do so in a unidirectional, hierarchical fashion.
evidence: This is a theoretical inference about the relationship between prediction reconciliation and EVC calculation.

claim: An overarching optimization procedure may simultaneously consider the costs and benefits of multiple cognitive control processes across different levels in the hierarchy.
source: More generally, in light of recent theoretic proposals of the hierarchical architecture of cognitive control (Koechlin and Summerfield, 2007; Badre and Nee, 2018), an overarching optimization procedure may simultaneously consider the costs and benefits of multiple cognitive control processes across different levels in the hierarchy, in order to guide goal-directed behavior while taking into account both the benefit and the cost of engaging cognitive control.
evidence: This is speculation about a general optimization framework, supported by citations to hierarchical control theories.

claim: The final sample consisted of 22 subjects (15 females; 22–35 years old, mean age = 27 years).
source: The final sample consisted of 22 subjects (15 females; 22–35 years old, mean age = 27 years).
evidence: This is a direct report of sample characteristics.

claim: Data from six subjects were excluded from further analysis due to low (<50%) accuracy in at least one of the cells in the experimental design.
source: Data from six subjects were excluded from further analysis due to low (<50%) accuracy in at least one of the cells in the experimental design (see below).
evidence: This is a direct report of exclusion criteria.

claim: This study was approved by the Duke University Health System Institutional Review Board.
source: This study was approved by the Duke University Health System Institutional Review Board.
evidence: This is a statement of ethical approval.

claim: The main task consisted of 9 runs of 50 trials each.
source: The main task consisted of 9 runs of 50 trials each.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental design.

claim: The sequences of tasks were pseudo-randomly produced so that the tasks performed on previous trials had no predictive power on the task to be performed on the current trial.
source: Importantly, the sequences of tasks were pseudo-randomly produced so that the tasks performed on previous trials had no predictive power on the task to be performed on the current trial.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental design.

claim: A stair-case procedure adaptively and separately adjusted the noise levels for color and motion to achieve accuracy of ~87.5% for both color and motion trials.
source: The practice session was followed by a stair-case procedure (4 runs of 50 trials each) that adaptively and separately adjusted the noise levels for color and motion to achieve accuracy of ~87.5% for both color and motion trials (cf. Waskom et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a direct description of the stair-case procedure.

claim: Error trials and outlier trials (RTs outside subject mean ±3 SDs) were removed from further analyses.
source: Error trials and outlier trials (RTs outside subject mean ±3 SDs) were removed from further analyses.
evidence: This is a direct description of data preprocessing.

claim: A nonnegative constraint was applied to the coefficients in the GLM models.
source: Based on the observation that larger PE slows down responses (Waskom et al., 2017), a nonnegative constraint was applied to the coefficients (Chiu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a direct description of the modeling approach, justified by citation.

claim: Functional images were scanned using a T2*-weighted single-shot gradient EPI sequence of 42 contiguous axial slices.
source: Functional images were scanned using a T2*-weighted single-shot gradient EPI sequence of 42 contiguous axial slices (slice thickness = 3 mm, TR = 2 s, TE = 28 ms, flip angle = 90°, FoV = 192 mm * 192 mm, in-plane resolution = 3 mm * 3 mm).
evidence: This is a direct description of MRI acquisition parameters.

claim: Preprocessing was done using SPM8.
source: Preprocessing was done using SPM8 http://www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm/.
evidence: This is a direct description of preprocessing software.

claim: Normalized images were smoothed using a Gaussian kernel with 5 mm full-width-half-maximum to increase signal.
source: Normalized images were then smoothed using a Gaussian kernel with 5 mm full-width-half-maximum to increase signal (Xue et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a direct description of preprocessing steps, justified by citation.

claim: Single trial fMRI activity levels at the onset of the pre-cue were estimated separately following Mumford et al. (2012).
source: Single trial fMRI activity levels at the onset of the pre-cue were estimated separately following Mumford et al. (2012) by regressing the fMRI signals against a GLM consisting of HRF–convolved onsets of the pre-cue at the trial, the onsets of all other pre-cues, and the onsets of all task stimuli.
evidence: This is a direct description of the analysis method, supported by citation.

claim: Searchlight-based MVPAs were conducted on a grey matter mask that was generated by dilating GM voxels in the segmented T1 template by 1 voxel.
source: We conducted searchlight-based (r = 2 voxels) MVPAs to quantify the representation strength of a given variable (e.g., Pcue). MVPAs were conducted on a grey matter (GM) mask that was generated by dilating GM voxels (GM value >0.01) in the segmented T1 template by 1 voxel (Jiang et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is a direct description of the MVPA procedure.

claim: The fitting in MVPA took the form of a ridge regression to control for over-fitting.
source: The fitting took the form of a ridge regression (Xue et al., 2010) to control for over-fitting.
evidence: This is a direct description of the MVPA fitting procedure, justified by citation.

claim: Group-level results were corrected using a non-parametric approach that randomly permutated the data for 10,000 times.
source: To correct for multiple comparisons, group-level results were corrected using a non-parametric approach (https://afni.nimh.nih.gov/pub/dist/doc/program_help/3dClustSim.html) that randomly permutated the data for 10,000 times, in order to generate a robust null distribution of the statistical map.
evidence: This is a direct description of the multiple comparison correction procedure.

claim: When voxelwise threshold was set at p<0.001 and family-wise error rate was set at 0.05, the cluster size thresholds ranged from 16 to 23 searchlights.
source: When voxelwise threshold was set at p<0.001 and family-wise error rate was set at 0.05, this approach yielded cluster size thresholds ranging from 16 to 23 searchlights, depending on the specific analysis.
evidence: This is a direct report of the statistical thresholds used.
